resident.chief_complaint: Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months in a 41-year-old female with no history of trauma.
resident.history: A 41-year-old female with no history of trauma presented with weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months. Initial cervical noncontrast MRI showed a hyperintense intramedullary cord signal, with differential diagnoses including cervical spondylotic myelopathy and tumor. She was referred for an open biopsy of the cervical spinal cord to document the pathology of the tumor. At the time of transfer, she had severe spastic quadriparesis, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Follow-up MRI revealed cervical spondylosis with C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression associated with an extensive intramedullary high cord signal and cord enlargement on T2-weighted sagittal images extending from C5 to C7; axial images confirmed the intramedullary signal abnormality. T1-weighted MRI sagittal scan showed the lesion enhanced with contrast at the C5–C6 level.
resident.physical_exam: On examination at the time of transfer, severe spastic quadriparesis was present, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction were reported in the history. Detailed motor power, reflexes, sensation, and sphincter examination findings are not documented in the record.

imaging.public_message: I have not seen the films and am reporting only the case record's imaging description: cervical spondylosis with cord compression at C5-6 and C6-7, with extensive intramedullary T2 high signal and cord enlargement from C5 to C7. The record does not state compression direction or stenosis grade. These reported findings correlate highly with the described progressive myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord lesion at C5–C7, likely intramedullary, producing upper motor neuron signs in all four limbs. The upper extremity predominance suggests central cord involvement. Detailed motor, reflex, sensory, and sphincter examination findings are not documented, limiting precise localization.

red_flags.finding: Intramedullary cord enlargement and contrast enhancement at C5–C6 on MRI
red_flags.rationale: This suggests an intrinsic cord lesion (e.g., tumor, demyelination, inflammation) that could independently cause the progressive myelopathy; surgical decompression for spondylotic compression may not address the primary pathology, and biopsy or medical management may be needed.

In compressive cervical myelopathy from C5–C7 spondylosis, lower extremities are typically more affected due to longer corticospinal tracts; upper extremity predominance suggests a central cord or intramedullary process, reinforcing the likelihood of a primary cord lesion rather than compression alone.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The imaging shows C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression, but the clinical pattern of upper extremity-predominant spastic quadriparesis is atypical for compressive cervical myelopathy at those levels, which would be expected to affect lower limbs more; additionally, cord enlargement and contrast enhancement are not typical for simple spondylotic compression, suggesting an intramedullary lesion that better explains the symptoms.
neurology.public_message: Localization: cervical spinal cord (C5–C7), with upper motor neuron signs in all four limbs. The imaging correlates with myelopathy but also shows an enhancing intramedullary lesion. Match level: medium. Red flags: (1) Enhancing intramedullary lesion (changes_indication) - may be the primary cause, not spondylotic compression. (2) Upper extremity-predominant weakness (changes_indication) - atypical for compression, supports intrinsic cord pathology. No other red flags.

physiatrist_opening.public_message: I remain the strongest advocate for conservative care. Given the progressive myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction, surgery is being considered, but before proceeding to irreversible intervention, I propose a formal, time-limited 3-6 month trial of intensive conservative management under close neurological monitoring. This would include supervised physical therapy for gait/balance/strength, occupational therapy for activities of daily living, cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, and avoidance of high-risk activities. The literature on nonoperative management of cervical spondylotic myelopathy reports that a subset of patients—particularly those with mild symptoms and no rapid progression—can stabilize or improve without surgery; however, I acknowledge that severe spastic quadriparesis with sphincter involvement and cord enhancement indicates a poorer prognosis for conservative care. Therefore, I define failure as any of the following: (1) no improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of strict conservative therapy; (2) new or worsening neurological deficits during the trial; (3) progression of intramedullary signal abnormality or enhancement on follow-up MRI at 3 months; or (4) inability to participate in therapy due to pain or functional decline. If any of these occur, I will accept that conservative management has failed and support surgical intervention or biopsy as appropriate. Until then, I hold my stance for a trial of conservative care.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The Deputy Director cited the enhancing intramedullary lesion and rapid progression with sphincter involvement as reasons not to delay. Those findings are already central to my position: they are why I set a conservative success rate of only 30% and included strict failure criteria, including no improvement or deterioration after 3 months and progression of enhancement on follow-up MRI. They justify close monitoring, but they do not yet outweigh the case for a carefully supervised trial before irreversible surgery, because no data show that a 3-month trial with predefined stopping rules would worsen outcome compared with immediate surgery. The record has not provided a comparison of outcomes for this specific constellation. I therefore hold my stance. I continue to propose a 3-6 month structured conservative program with early stopping if any failure criterion is met.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 41-year-old woman with progressive cervical myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction over 2 months. Imaging demonstrates cord compression at C5-6 and C6-7 with extensive T2 hyperintensity, cord enlargement, and focal contrast enhancement at C5-6. The clinical and radiological picture is most consistent with myelopathy from combined spondylotic compression and possible intrinsic cord lesion (neoplastic or inflammatory). Severe spastic quadriparesis with sphincter dysfunction indicates significant cord injury, and delay risks irreversible deficit. However, the enhancing intramedullary lesion complicates the etiology and may not be fully addressed by decompression alone.
proposed_options: Immediate surgical decompression (e.g., anterior or posterior approach based on final imaging review) with intraoperative open biopsy of the enhancing intramedullary lesion.

Further diagnostic workup prior to surgery: CSF analysis including cytology and oligoclonal bands, serum inflammatory/infectious markers, review of MRI with contrast and potentially additional sequences (e.g., diffusion, MR spectroscopy), and neuro-oncology consultation; then plan surgery if no contraindication.

Conservative management trial as proposed by physiatry, with very close neurological monitoring, only if the director judges the risk of surgical intervention to outweigh the risk of progression; I would note this carries high risk of irreversible deterioration.
disagreement_points: I am concerned that a 3-6 month conservative trial is inappropriate given severe progressive quadriparesis and sphincter dysfunction; the risk of irreversible deficit outweighs the potential to avoid surgery.

The enhancing intramedullary lesion may represent tumor, demyelination, or inflammatory myelitis; decompression alone would not treat an intrinsic lesion, and open biopsy may be necessary, but biopsy also carries risks.
The record lacks key information (past medical history, laboratory results, exact stenosis grade and compression direction) that would help differentiate the etiology and surgical urgency.
deferred_questions_to_director: Should we proceed directly to surgical decompression with biopsy, or obtain additional diagnostic studies first, and how long can we safely delay?
Would you prefer a combined decompression and biopsy in one procedure, or a staged approach beginning with biopsy?
Do you want any further imaging or medical consultations before the surgical plan is final?
vice_opinions.public_message: Director, this case has two overlapping problems: severe cervical stenosis with cord compression and an enhancing intramedullary lesion. The patient's rapid progression with sphincter involvement makes delay risky. I would not support a prolonged conservative trial, but the need to diagnose the enhancing lesion before definitive surgery is uncertain. I would appreciate your guidance on whether to proceed with decompression and biopsy now or to obtain further diagnostic workup first, and on the surgical approach.

director_rulings.final_decision: Close the meeting pending further diagnostic workup. Do not operate today. I order additional imaging and laboratory studies to rule out an intrinsic cord lesion, demyelinating or inflammatory disease, and to stratify surgical risk. The department will reconvene after results are available and after a family meeting to discuss options with detailed informed consent. If the workup confirms cervical spondylotic myelopathy without a medically treatable cause, the planned operation will be posterior decompression with biopsy under intraoperative neuromonitoring; contingency plans for difficult airway, intraoperative hypotension, and CSF leak must be confirmed with anesthesia. The radiologist, anesthesiologist, physiatrist, neurologist, and resident have been asked to complete the delegated tasks.
delegated_tasks: Radiologist: review the actual cervical MRI images and report stenosis grade, direction of compression, and enhancement pattern.
Anesthesiologist: perform a preoperative airway assessment and provide a risk stratification for prone positioning and hemodynamic management.
Physiatrist: document baseline functional status and the predefined conservative trial failure criteria in the chart.
Neurologist: interpret the CSF and autoimmune panel results and advise on whether medical therapy is indicated.
Resident: obtain complete past medical history, family history, prior laboratory results, and arrange the ordered tests.
director_rulings.reason_for_delay: Diagnostic workup and a family meeting are required before any surgical decision to avoid irreversible intervention on an undiagnosed enhancing intramedullary lesion and to obtain informed consent.
